extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics, mathematicians and graduate students interested in foundations and history of analysis
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly examination of Cauchy’s notions of rigor, limit, continuity, infinitesimals, and his sum theorem, contrasting two interpretive 'tracks' (A-track: Archimedean/ε-δ; B-track: variable quantities/infinitesimals) and providing modern formalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of rigor (Cauchy: 'all the rigor one demands from geometry')
rubrics_metrics.description: Cauchy committed in his introduction to 'all the rigor one demands from geometry' and to 'never rely on arguments taken from the generality of algebra.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interprets Cauchy's intended standard as Euclidean-geometry-level precision rather than the later 19th-century ε-δ 'rigorization'; implies avoiding certain algebraic generalities (see next entry) and privileging geometric-style precision in proofs and definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of the 'generality of algebra'
rubrics_metrics.description: Generality of algebra refers to techniques (1) proofs based on algebraic manipulation of divergent series, and (2) the idea that algebraic rules and formulas valid in the real domain remain valid in the complex domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those techniques are characterized as 'cavalier' by Cauchy's standards; historically some such proofs were later justified by summation methods or analytic continuation, but Cauchy's dictum counsels caution in using these algebraic shortcuts as foundational arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of limit in terms of variable quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: Cauchy's definition: 'When the values successively attributed to a particular variable indefinitely approach a fixed value in such a way as to end up by differing from it by as little as we wish, this fixed value is called the limit of all the other values.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits are presented with variable quantities primary; the notation 'lim.' is treated as an abbreviation secondary to the concept of variable quantities. Track-A reads this as equivalent to null sequences; Track-B reads it as indicating a change of nature (variable → infinitesimal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitesimals as variable quantities with limit zero
rubrics_metrics.description: Cauchy's characterization: 'When the successive numerical values of such a variable decrease indefinitely, in such a way as to fall below any given number, this variable becomes what we call infinitesimal, or an infinitely small quantity. A variable of this kind has zero as its limit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two readings: A-track treats an infinitesimal as a null sequence; B-track emphasizes the verb 'becomes' (a variable becomes infinitesimal), suggesting a conceptual change and inassignable quantities. The ambiguity is important for interpreting Cauchy's use in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity via commutation of function and limit (1817 characterisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1817 characterisation: 'The limit of a continuous function of several variables is [equal to] the same function of their limit,' expressed succinctly as ϕ ◦ lim = lim ◦ ϕ at a point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This commutation view of continuity (sequence/limit formulation) is used by Cauchy in proofs (e.g., functional equations, intermediate value theorem) and contrasts with his later infinitesimal-based definitions in CDA. It can be transcribed directly into modern sequence-based continuity (ϕ(lim xn)=lim ϕ(xn)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity via infinitesimal increments (1821 definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cauchy's 1821 CDA definition: for each x between given limits, if an infinitesimal increment α is added to x then the difference f(x+α)−f(x) 'decreases indefinitely' with the numerical value of α; equivalently 'an infinitely small increment in the variable always produces an infinitely small increment in the function itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This infinitesimal formulation reappears in later works (1823, 1829, 1844, 1853). It serves as an intermediary between the 1817 commutation definition and a pure infinitesimal approach. Modern nonstandard formalizations render it equivalent (at standard points) to ε-δ continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform convergence / 'always' condition for sum theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Cauchy's 1821 sum theorem (as originally stated) implied pointwise convergence of a series of continuous functions yields a continuous sum; by 1853 he added that the sum un+...+un'−1 'always becomes infinitely small for infinitely large values of n and n' > n.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars interpret the 1853 'always' as effectively requiring uniform convergence. A-track reads it as independence of n,n' and x (a modern uniform quantifier: ∀ε ∃N ∀n,n'≥N ∀x ...), while B-track reads 'always' as applying to inassignable (nonstandard/infinitesimal) inputs as well. Counterexamples (Abel) show the 1821 statement is false without the uniformity condition; Cauchy's evaluation at x=1/n illustrates the need to consider nonstandard inputs in the B-track reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstandard/SPOT formalization: infinitesimal criterion equivalent to ε-δ for standard points
rubrics_metrics.description: Using SPOT (a conservative nonstandard framework), 'Let x be a standard point... Then f is continuous at x (in the traditional ε-δ sense) iff infinitesimal α produce infinitesimal changes f(x+α)−f(x),' with continuity on an interval equivalent to this holding for every standard point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a modern formal bridge between Cauchy's infinitesimal language and ε-δ continuity without relying on the Axiom of Choice or ultrafilters. It also clarifies distinctions between continuity, uniform continuity, and the role of standard vs nonstandard inputs in reading Cauchy's 'always' clause.
